card.hook: Tiananmen Square is so big that your phone will struggle to take it all in. Don't fight it. Pick one thing, like the gate, the monument or the flag, and let all that empty space do the bragging.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, about 55 m west of the subject, and face east. Stay out on the open ground rather than close to the buildings, so you can fit more in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the full width of the square, then switch to 1x for a natural view of a single building. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the gate, the flag or the monument from far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon and building edges straight, and tap the main building, then drag the slider to make it a bit darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are when the flag is raised and lowered, so you get real atmosphere, though expect a crowd. Early or late in the day the light is also softer than at midday.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Golden Water Bridges, on the square side, so the Tiananmen Rostrum and the Mao portrait are behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it slightly up so the gate sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the square side of the road, facing north toward Tiananmen Gate, while you stand in front of the gate, so the whole gate is framed symmetrically.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are banned on the square. Selfie sticks are a mixed story: some guides say they're confiscated at security and others say you can bring one, so check before you go (and the entry rules can change too). Watch out for scams, including people who offer to take your photo, so pick your own helper.
card.challenge: Take one shot of a single subject with lots of empty space around it, and include just a few people so everyone can see how huge the square is.
card.good_to_know: The square was first laid out in 1651 and made about four times bigger in the 1950s. It now measures roughly 765 by 282 metres. Together with the Central Axis, it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2024.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon on the map, about 55 m west of the subject, and face east. Stay out on the open ground rather than close to the buildings, so you can fit more in.

card.hook: Down at street level, the Forbidden City is simply too big for your phone, so don't fight it. Climb a hill instead and let the whole palace spread out below you.
card.stand_here: Head to 万春亭, the pavilion at the summit of Jingshan Hill, and stand on its south side. Face south, and the palace lies straight ahead; the climb from the park's south entrance takes roughly 10 to 15 minutes.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the main view. If the full width of the palace won't fit, go to 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out roofs and gates in the middle distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the central axis up with the middle of the frame, then tap the palace and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon before sunset or early morning works best, and one guide says the hour before sunset gives the warmest light. The rail gets busiest around sunset, so arrive early in that hour to grab a spot.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x so more of the view squeezes in, and hold the phone a little high with the view behind you over your shoulder. Take a few, because someone's elbow will sneak into at least one.
card.rules_and_safety: Jingshan Park charges an entrance fee, and the Palace Museum manages entry to the Forbidden City itself, so check the official sites for current prices and rules before you go. Hold your phone against the rail or your body to keep it steady.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one zoomed-in shot of the halls, then pan a slow panorama that catches the White Pagoda of Beihai too.
card.good_to_know: The Forbidden City was the imperial palace of the Ming and Qing emperors, built between 1406 and 1420. Twenty-four emperors lived there until 1924. It covers about 72 hectares, now runs as the Palace Museum, and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to 万春亭, the pavilion at the summit of Jingshan Hill, and stand on its south side. Face south, and the palace lies straight ahead; the climb from the park's south entrance takes roughly 10 to 15 minutes.

card.hook: Picture a long stone path rising gently toward a round blue roof, with everything lined up like someone used a ruler. That's the Temple of Heaven from the Vermilion Steps Bridge, and it's a lot of fun to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of the Vermilion Steps Bridge (Danbi Bridge, 丹陛桥) and face north toward the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. The bridge runs between the Imperial Vault of Heaven and the Hall, so the Hall sits at the far end of your view.
card.zoom: Try zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) so the long bridge and the Hall squeeze together. If your phone stops at 1x, that works too. Save zoom 0.5x for a low, dramatic shot of the stone path.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the centre of the path on the middle vertical line, tap the blue roof, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out the tiles.
card.best_time: Check how busy it is on the day, since people keep walking across the bridge. The Hall can't be entered after about 6 pm, but you can still photograph it from outside when it's lit. One guide says the park lights up on Friday and Saturday nights at 8 pm, so check before you rely on that. For evening shots, use night mode and hold your phone steady against a railing or your body.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Danbi Bridge itself with the Temple of Heaven behind you. The long central path adds depth, so use the front camera (and 0.5x if your phone offers it) and keep the Hall over your shoulder. For a quieter backdrop, try the red wall on the east or west side of the Hall of Prayer, away from the busy front.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the bridge's central line looking toward the Hall of Prayer, while you stand a little way ahead of them so the blue roof sits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are allowed, but keep them under about 1.3 m and don't stretch one out where it blocks a walkway. Hold it in your hand and follow any staff signs. You need a ticket for the park and its halls, and some areas may be closed for works, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the Hall dead centre and the path perfectly straight, with not a single stranger's elbow in the frame. Take a few shots in a row and see how many tries it takes.
card.good_to_know: The Ming and Qing emperors came here to pray for good harvests. It was first built in 1420, its layout was largely settled by 1749, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998. The Hall of Prayer is 38 m tall and the park covers about 2.73 square kilometres, so choose your pictures and keep your phone's camera clean.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of the Vermilion Steps Bridge (Danbi Bridge, 丹陛桥) and face north toward the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. The bridge runs between the Imperial Vault of Heaven and the Hall, so the Hall sits at the far end of your view.

card.hook: At 1x, one of China's most famous buildings shows up on your phone as a thin red-and-yellow stripe across a very big square. Don't worry, a quick zoom fixes it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map in Tiananmen Square, about 440 m south of the subject, and face north. From here the whole width of the gate and its double roof fits in one frame.
card.zoom: Zoom 5x if your phone has it, otherwise 2x, until the gate fills about half the width of the screen. Take one more shot at 1x so you also get the square around it.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red wall, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the yellow roof tiles.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows, and early in the day is often quieter. Try to skip the midday haze.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Golden Water Bridges (the Jinshui Bridge area) at the north end of the square and try the gate tower behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if you have it, hold the phone a bit higher and see what fits when you get there.

card.rules_and_safety: Guides disagree on whether selfie sticks are allowed through security, so they may be confiscated. Don't photograph on-duty police, armed guards or soldiers, and don't point your phone at them on purpose. Check the official site first, as there may be security checks and reservations are needed for entry.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal line, with Mao's portrait right in the middle. Can you get it dead level?
card.good_to_know: The first gate on this spot dates from 1420 in the Ming dynasty. It burned down and was rebuilt more than once, and it took the name Tiananmen in 1651. The building is about 66 m long, 37 m wide and 32 m high, and in 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China from its balcony.

card.hook: Picture a giant nest of grey steel twigs lighting up at dusk, with a second one glowing upside down in the lake. That's the Bird's Nest, and it looks like nothing else in Beijing.
card.stand_here: Don't stand at the phone icon, because that marks the middle of the stadium itself. Walk to the lakeside on the north side of the dragon-shaped water system and face the stadium across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close to the water, so the whole stadium and its reflection fit. Switch to 1x for a natural view, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the steel pattern or the Olympic Tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on a lower line, so the stadium and its reflection fill the picture and the building stays level.
card.best_time: Go around dusk, just as the stadium lights come on. Wait a few minutes after they switch on, while the sky still has some colour. If you arrive earlier, South Gate Square gives a classic front-on view in soft daylight.
card.selfie_here: Head to the water's edge on the southeast side of the stadium, where several guides say the lit Bird's Nest reflects best at night. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the stadium over your shoulder. The open plaza in front of the main facade is another good spot, with the steel structure right behind you.
card.ask_someone: On Datu Road Bridge, ask a passer-by to take a wide shot of you with the whole Bird's Nest behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: At the security check, selfie sticks aren't allowed through, but they can be checked and stored. If you go up to the rooftop walkway, the wind is strong, so don't lean over the railings for a shot.
card.challenge: Can you fit the Bird's Nest, its reflection, and the Water Cube or Olympic Tower into one frame?
card.good_to_know: The Bird's Nest was built for the 2008 Summer Olympics and opened on 28 June 2008. It holds around 80,000 people and was used again for the 2022 Winter Olympics. The Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron studied Chinese ceramics while designing it.

card.hook: This building is about 356 metres long, so the first challenge is simply fitting it on your screen. The second is doing it without half of Beijing walking through your shot.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole facade and the row of columns. Switch to 1x for the entrance, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the national emblem under the eaves.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: We don't have a best hour for this one, so just allow extra time for security queues. Expect crowds, take a few frames, and be patient.
card.selfie_here: Go to the steps at the front entrance, in front of the marble columns, with the building behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the columns fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand in the middle of Tiananmen Square near the Monument to the People's Heroes, and ask a passer-by to take your picture with the hall behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Security checks are strict, and photography in the square is restricted, so take photos only in designated areas. Selfie sticks are allowed only in designated areas and must be no longer than 1.3 metres.
card.challenge: Take the classic full-front shot once, then find the quieter angle and compare. Which one has fewer strangers in it?
card.good_to_know: The Great Hall opened in September 1959 as one of the "Ten Great Constructions" for the tenth anniversary of the People's Republic. The building work took only ten months. It's about 356 metres long and 206.5 metres wide, and rises to 46.5 metres at its highest point. China's National People's Congress meets here each March.

card.hook: Red walls, golden roof tiles and carved timber are all squeezed in together here, so your phone barely has to try. Even a quick snap looks like a postcard.
card.stand_here: Stand at 雍和门, right below the entrance archway, and face in toward the courtyard. The gate frames the red walls and golden roofs in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole courtyard and its buildings into one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for roof tiles, eaves and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the golden roof tiles, then slide it a bit darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the colours.
card.best_time: Go early on a weekday morning, when it's quietest. Weekends, Chinese holidays and the 1st and 15th of the lunar month are the busiest.
card.selfie_here: Stand against the red wall on the right side of the main entrance once you've bought your incense. It's a bold colour backdrop with the entrance area behind you. For fewer people, try the red wall beside the Pavilion of Ten Thousand Happinesses (Wanfuge). Use the front camera, or 0.5x for a full-body shot, with the roofline over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo in the courtyard in front of Dacheng Hall, ideally in golden hour light, so the whole temple fills the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine outside the halls but not inside them, and not of the Buddha statues in the Wanfu Pavilion, so check the signs. Skip the flash, and don't photograph monks or other visitors without asking. If you wander to the peach trees on the sidewalk outside the northern wall, watch for cyclists and pedestrians.
card.challenge: Get the red walls on both sides and the golden roofs across the top, all in one straight, gridline-perfect shot.
card.good_to_know: This is a working Tibetan Buddhist monastery, and building began in 1694 as a princely residence. The future Yongzheng Emperor lived here before he took the throne. Under the Qianlong Emperor the roofs got yellow tiles, a colour reserved for the emperor, and in 1744 the palace became a monastery.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at 雍和门, right below the entrance archway, and face in toward the courtyard. The gate frames the red walls and golden roofs in front of you.

card.hook: You've puffed up a load of stone steps, and then the whole Forbidden City unrolls at your feet like a roof-shaped carpet. That's the Jingshan moment, and it's worth the climb.
card.stand_here: Stand at the summit pavilion, 万春亭, right at the south-facing centre point of the summit. Face south so the palace rooftops stretch away along the central axis in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic south-facing view. If the railing is packed and you're stuck in a corner, go to 0.5x to fit in more roofs and sky, or try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out single halls.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the roofs, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Get there well before sunset so you can grab a spot at the railing, then aim for the hour before sunset for warm light. It's busy at sunset and at weekends, and the railing fills up late in the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to the south-facing railing at the top of Wanchun Pavilion, where the palace lies below. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the rooftops over your shoulder. It shows the palace more than the park itself. For a quieter shot, try the red-walled courtyard near Shouhuang Hall at the northern foot of the hill, which is less crowded than the summit.
card.ask_someone: Near the South Gate, across the street from Shenwu Gate, ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand on the park side of the road with the entrance and hill in view.
card.rules_and_safety: There's an entrance charge, and the summit is reached by stone steps, so it isn't step-free. Check the official site for opening hours and gate rules before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo facing south, then turn round and spot the Drum and Bell Towers to the north. Can you get both in under a minute?
card.good_to_know: Jingshan is a Ming-dynasty hill, about 45.7 metres high, built from soil dug out when the palace moats and nearby canals were made. It has five peaks, each with a pavilion, and together they mark the rough line of Beijing's central axis. The park opened to the public in 1928.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the summit pavilion, 万春亭, right at the south-facing centre point of the summit. Face south so the palace rooftops stretch away along the central axis in front of you.

card.hook: This hall just sits out in the open in the middle of Tiananmen Square, about 160 m across, with nothing in front of it but paving and passing visitors. That makes it one of the easiest big buildings to fit in a photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open ground of Tiananmen Square in front of the hall's main entrance, with the Tiananmen gate and Mao portrait behind you to the north. Face south, toward the hall.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole building in. Go to 2x or 3x for the columns and roofline if it feels too far away. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of open square around the hall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the base of the building on a lower line so the roofline sits level, and leave some paving in front to show how big the square is.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people than midday. Check the official site for the day's access arrangements before you plan your visit.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the square just outside the hall's entrance, with the hall behind you. Use the front camera, or switch to 0.5x if the building won't fit. The sculpted memorials beside the hall are another spot if you can get the hall in the frame behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the open square near the entrance with the hall behind you, and ask a passer-by to step back across the paving, face the hall and frame you in the middle.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos and video aren't allowed inside the hall. Bags aren't allowed in the mausoleum either, and there's a cloakroom across the street. Drones aren't permitted on the square. Rules can change, so check signage on the day, and please be respectful, since people come here to pay their respects.
card.challenge: Get the roofline dead level on a gridline, with a few strangers walking through the frame for scale.
card.good_to_know: The hall is the final resting place of Mao Zedong and stands on the site of the Gate of China, the southern main gate of the Imperial City in the Ming and Qing dynasties. It was finished on 24 May 1977, with granite from Sichuan and pine trees from Yan'an. It closed for nine months of renovation in 1997 and reopened on 6 January 1998.

card.hook: The National Museum of China is 313 metres of calm stone with ten square pillars in the middle, and it makes you feel wonderfully tiny. That's the fun of it, and it's why a plain phone photo works so well here.
card.stand_here: Head to the front steps of the National Museum of China (中国国家博物馆) on the square side, a short walk from the phone icon. Face across Tiananmen Square towards the Great Hall of the People and the Monument to the People's Heroes.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the Great Hall across the square, then go to 0.5x when you want the whole open square. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Monument to the People's Heroes.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the horizon level so the big buildings don't lean, and put the Monument or the Great Hall on one third line with open square in front.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, close to the 5 PM closing time, when the light turns warm. Visitors often sit on these steps at the end of the day to shoot the buildings opposite, but the light varies, so check it on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try the east railings of the square, using the front camera. A 2x zoom can help keep other visitors out of the frame. It's a low-confidence pick, so we can't promise the museum sits behind you. Check your screen and shuffle until the long columned building is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out on the square facing the museum's columned facade, and you stand in front of it, so people walking past show how big it is.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the museum, flash and selfie sticks aren't allowed, and temporary exhibitions follow the signs in each gallery. Drones aren't allowed on the square either, so brace your elbows on the steps or a railing to keep your phone steady.
card.challenge: Fit all ten pillars in one shot with a tiny person walking past for scale. Bonus points if they don't notice they're your model.
card.good_to_know: The museum was finished in 1959 as one of the Ten Great Buildings marking ten years of the People's Republic, built to balance the Great Hall of the People opposite. It reopened in March 2011 after four years of renovation. Its front has also carried countdown clocks before big national occasions, including the 2008 Beijing Olympics. The square outside is public, but going inside needs advance booking with a passport, so check the official site first.

card.hook: Picture a bright white stupa sitting on an island above the trees, with a whole lake to frame it. It's about the easiest landmark in Beijing to spot, and it looks great on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Five Dragon Pavilions (五龙亭) on the lake's north shore and look across the water to the White Dagoba on Qionghua Island. The centre of Beihai Park is to the south-east of here.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the water and the dagoba together. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the dagoba closer without walking. Save 0.5x for when you're right by the pavilions and want their roofs to fill the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dagoba, then slide the brightness down a little so the white stone keeps its detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or in the late afternoon, when the light is soft. Guides often say late light is when the dagoba looks its best.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with the dagoba right behind you, climb up to its stone base on Jade Island, using the steps up from the causeway that starts at the north gate entrance. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and keep the dagoba over your shoulder. At the Five Dragon Pavilions the dagoba may end up in front of you instead, so check the angle on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the south side of Yong'an Bridge and frame you with the White Dagoba behind you for its front view.
card.rules_and_safety: Beihai Park bans commercial photography teams with big gear like extra lights and reflectors, but you can still take your own photos, even in traditional clothing. The inner gardens are reported closed on Mondays, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the dagoba on an upper third with the water level along the bottom, then see if you can spot a ripple-free frame in your Live Photo.
card.good_to_know: Beihai Park is a former imperial garden just northwest of the Forbidden City, and it has been open to the public since 1925. The lake covers more than half of its roughly 71 hectares. The White Dagoba is about 40 metres high and was built in 1651 to honour a visit by the 5th Dalai Lama.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Five Dragon Pavilions (五龙亭) on the lake's north shore and look across the water to the White Dagoba on Qionghua Island. The centre of Beihai Park is to the south-east of here.

card.hook: Picture a white Romanesque church with twin spires sitting at the end of a street packed with shops, with glass mall towers rising right behind it. That clash of old and new is why everyone stops here.
card.stand_here: Stand right in front of St. Joseph's Catholic Church (the East Church), on the front plaza by the lawn, at the north end of Wangfujing pedestrian street. Face the church, with the main street running away to the south behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole church and plaza. If you're close and the spires won't fit, go to 0.5x. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the brickwork and spire details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the spires up with the vertical lines so they stand up straight, with a strip of lawn at the bottom for depth.
card.best_time: Come around sunset and stay into blue hour, when the church lights come on. One guide says about 5:30 PM, but that shifts with the season, so check the sunset time for your date.
card.selfie_here: For a night selfie, stand in the middle of the pedestrian street with the lit-up street glowing behind you, using your front camera. If you want the skyline instead, the WF Central rooftop (269 Wangfujing Street) frames old and new Beijing behind you, but check it's open before you go.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the north end of the pedestrian street and shoot south, so you and the whole length of the lit-up street fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The church exterior is free to photograph, but the inside has fixed visiting times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get both spires dead straight on the gridlines with nobody's head sticking up in front of them? Plaza crowds say no.
card.good_to_know: Wangfujing means 'prince's residence well', named after a well of sweet water found among the Qing-dynasty princes' homes. Until the late 1990s the street had traffic, and changes in 1999 and 2000 made most of it pedestrian only. It now has around 280 shops, and the snack street just to the west sells kebabs and candied fruit on sticks.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right in front of St. Joseph's Catholic Church (the East Church), on the front plaza by the lawn, at the north end of Wangfujing pedestrian street. Face the church, with the main street running away to the south behind you.

card.hook: Picture a row of moored boats, a soft layer of rooftops and the sun sliding down toward the Western Hills. That's the Yinding Bridge view, and it's so famous it's one of the Eight Views of Yanjing, "Yinding Viewing the Mountains".
card.stand_here: Stand on 银锭桥 (Yinding Bridge), on the west side of the bridge. Face west along the water toward the Western Hills.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the bridge, lake and boats. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the hills and distant rooftops closer. If the bridge is packed, zoom 0.5x gets the whole lake and sky in.
card.make_it_pop: With the sun behind the scene, tap the bright sky, then slide the brightness down a little so the colours stay rich (or tap a boat if you want it brighter up front).
card.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset. One guide says after 3 PM, another says around 5 PM, and in winter golden hour is around 4:30 to 5 PM. It gets crowded at sunset, so arrive early and wait for a clear gap at the railing.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the bridge deck at Yinding Bridge, facing the lake and the sunset light on the water. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your phone a bit high so the lake and sky fit over your shoulder. For a different backdrop, the roof terrace at Tangfang Coffee (糖房咖啡) shows the lake and hutongs spread out behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Houhai lake shore, so you and Yinding Bridge with its old buildings fit in the same frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch your belongings at night. The café terrace has a minimum spend, and it's worth checking the official site for closures before you go.
card.challenge: Get a shot with a moored boat on the edge of the frame and the water line on a lower third, with no stranger's head in the way. Patience at the railing counts as part of the game.
card.good_to_know: Shichahai is three linked lakes (Qianhai, Xihai and Houhai) covering about 147 hectares, and it dates back to the Jin Dynasty. Under the Yuan Dynasty it was the northern end of the Grand Canal, so it became a busy trading district. The name means roughly "the lake of ten temples", and the shores still have temples, old mansions and tall trees.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on 银锭桥 (Yinding Bridge), on the west side of the bridge. Face west along the water toward the Western Hills.

card.hook: Nanluoguxiang's main lane is so busy that a clean, empty shot is nearly impossible. So skip the crush and walk to the north end, where a big red wall is waiting with far fewer people in front of it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Drum Tower at the north end of Nanluoguxiang, and head for the red walls at the side of the tower, not the crowded front. Face the walls so the tower's grey roofline sits above them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the red walls. If the side walls are too close to fit, tap 0.5x. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the grey roofline or a lantern without stepping into the crowd.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red wall, then drag the slider a little darker so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft daylight suits the red walls and grey brick. Check on the day for when the lane is quietest.
card.selfie_here: Try Mao'er Hutong, about 100 m west into the hutong from the main street, on the grey-brick lane near the bicycles at the doorways. Use the front camera and hold it a bit low, so the brick and bikes fill in behind you. A visitor guide says afternoon sun there looks lovely.
card.rules_and_safety: The lane and side streets are open public streets, and you can photograph the red walls at the side of the Drum Tower from the street.
card.challenge: Hunt down one lantern, doorway or rooftop detail, zoom in on it, and get it with zero people in the frame.
card.good_to_know: Nanluoguxiang is about 800 metres long and runs from Gulou East Street in the north to Di'anmen East Street in the south. It was built in the Yuan Dynasty and got its current name in the Qing Dynasty, around 1750. Today it's lined with cafés, bars, live music venues and souvenir shops, plus a few old courtyard houses linked to famous historic and literary figures.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Drum Tower at the north end of Nanluoguxiang, and head for the red walls at the side of the tower, not the crowded front. Face the walls so the tower's grey roofline sits above them.

card.hook: Walk north and the Drum Tower just keeps growing in front of you, roofline first. It's big, solid and impossible to lose, which makes it a great first photo of the day.
card.stand_here: Stand near 地安门外大街, at the phone icon on the map, about 70 m south of the Drum Tower. Face north and the whole building sits straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole tower in, with a bit of street for atmosphere. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the roof edges. Use zoom 0.5x only if you've moved closer and the tower won't fit.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on the centre line so both sides look balanced, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the colours than midday sun. If the light looks flat, wait for a brighter moment.
card.selfie_here: Go to Drum Tower West Street, directly beneath the south side of the tower on its west side, and lean on or hold one of the columns with the tower behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in the open square between the Drum Tower and the Bell Tower to take your photo, with the Drum Tower in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Take care crossing the street if you want the distant view from the first intersection on the west side. Opening and access aren't covered here, so check locally before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole tower, then a close one of just the roof edges, and see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: The Drum Tower is in central Beijing. Its solid, traditional shape makes it a strong subject, and the roofline is the part that catches the eye. It's big enough to stand out against the sky.

card.hook: Face north near Qianmen Avenue and a huge grey gate rises right in front of you, its tiered roofs towering over everything around it. It's so well balanced it almost photographs itself.
card.stand_here: Stand near 前门大街, at the phone icon on the map, about 200 m south of the subject, and face north. The gate should sit in the middle of your frame, with the archery tower possibly in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole gate and a bit of street. For a tighter shot, walk towards the gate rather than zooming in a lot. Use zoom 0.5x only if you've walked much closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the main gateway on the centre line, and keep your phone level so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the tower. Early in the day is also likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the open plaza straight in front of the gate, with the gate behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and let the tower rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the crosswalk and wide square in front of the archery tower, and ask your photographer to step back from the gate so the whole structure fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are generally restricted near major historical sites in Beijing, and one guide says drone photos here are highly unlikely to be allowed. Flash is generally prohibited inside museum exhibits, so follow posted signs. If you want to go inside the gatehouse, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get a perfectly symmetrical shot with the gateway dead centre, then see if you can catch a few people walking through for a sense of scale.
card.good_to_know: Zhengyangmen, better known as Qianmen, was first built in 1419 and the gate complex was heavily rebuilt in 1914. At 42 metres, it's the tallest gatehouse in Beijing's old city wall, and one of the few that still has its main tower. The city's central north–south axis runs through its main gate, which is why the view from the south looks so symmetrical.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near 前门大街, at the phone icon on the map, about 200 m south of the subject, and face north. The gate should sit in the middle of your frame, with the archery tower possibly in the foreground.

card.hook: Locals call this giant dome "the Boiled Egg", and the moment you reach the water's edge you'll see why. It sits in its own lake, so it's one smooth shape with nothing in the way.
card.stand_here: Walk around the lake to the east lakeshore, across the water from the building. It's a short walk around the lake, on foot. Face the dome across the water so the whole shell fills the view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the dome and its reflection. If the whole shell won't fit, tap 0.5x. Save zoom 2x to 5x for close-ups of the titanium surface or people on the far side.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dome or your subject, then slide the brightness a little darker so the lit shell keeps its colour and silhouettes stay dark.
card.best_time: Go at blue hour, roughly 6:30 to 7:30 pm, when the shell is lit and the sky still has some colour. That time shifts through the year, so treat it as a rough guide.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the east lakeshore with the egg-shaped dome filling the view behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the dome in, and keep it over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Head to the north side of the dome, by the main entrance, then hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to fit the whole dome and the Great Hall of the People in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Tripods and selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the venue. Going inside is ticketed and photos aren't allowed during performances, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Make a silhouette: put a friend (or yourself) against the lit shell and keep the whole figure in the frame, head to toe.
card.good_to_know: French architect Paul Andreu designed the dome, which opened in 2007. It's about 212 metres long and 46 metres high, made of more than 18,000 titanium plates with a band of glass up the middle. Visitors reach the halls through a long passage under the water, which is why nothing spoils the outline.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk around the lake to the east lakeshore, across the water from the building. It's a short walk around the lake, on foot. Face the dome across the water so the whole shell fills the view.

card.hook: The Monument to the People's Heroes stands completely alone in the middle of one of the biggest open squares around. There's nothing to hide behind and nothing to crop out, so it's an easy subject for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in the centre of Tiananmen Square (天安门广场), on the north or south approach. Face the obelisk and shoot along the line of the square, so Tiananmen Gate and the big state buildings frame it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the obelisk with the gate and buildings around it. Go to 0.5x if you want the whole open square. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the inscription and the carved panels from behind the barriers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, hold the phone upright and keep the sides of the monument parallel to the vertical lines, with a little empty sky above the top.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer. Avoid noon: strong backlight turns faces dark. Don't shoot straight into the sun, or the shadowed side of the stone goes dark too.
card.selfie_here: Try the open paving right next to the obelisk in Tiananmen Square, so it fills the frame behind you. The south side of the monument is said to be less crowded. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low so the tall obelisk fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed in Tiananmen Square. Expect a security check on the way in and big crowds. Barriers keep you back from the monument, so shoot from where you're allowed to stand.
card.challenge: Take one straight-on shot of the obelisk with the gate behind it, then one low, close-up shot of the granite and carved panels at the base. Which one do you like better?
card.good_to_know: The obelisk is ten storeys of granite and 37.94 metres tall. Architect Liang Sicheng led the design, and building ran from August 1952 to May 1958. The front carries Mao Zedong's handwritten inscription, 'Eternal glory to the people's heroes', and the base is inlaid with eight large and two small relief panels showing major events in modern Chinese history. It has been a nationally protected heritage site since 1961.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the centre of Tiananmen Square (天安门广场), on the north or south approach. Face the obelisk and shoot along the line of the square, so Tiananmen Gate and the big state buildings frame it.
